analysis.investment_thesis: Aegis Logistics owns irreplaceable liquid and gas terminal infrastructure in India — the kind of critical, permit-protected assets that cannot easily be replicated — and has compounded net profit at 22.6% CAGR over nine years. However, the capital intensity is high, finance costs are rising sharply (165 Cr in FY25 vs 17 Cr in FY21), and total debt has ballooned to 4,606 Cr against equity of 5,941 Cr, making the actual leverage meaningfully higher than the stated 0.28 D/E.
key_strengths: Durable infrastructure moat: LPG and liquid terminal assets require regulatory approvals, large capital, and years to build — competitors cannot simply appear overnight
Consistent profit growth: operating income grew at 21.9% CAGR over 9 years and net profit at 22.6% CAGR, with OCF positive all 5 of the last 5 years
58.1% promoter holding signals strong management alignment, and India's LPG infrastructure build-out provides a long multi-decade runway
key_risks: Total debt of 4,606 Cr (FY25) against equity of 5,941 Cr implies effective D/E close to 0.78 — far higher than the reported 0.28 — and finance costs of 165 Cr are growing at 27.9% CAGR, eating into future profitability
FCF is largely negative due to sustained capex (945 Cr in FY25 alone), meaning the business depends on external financing to fund growth, increasing balance sheet risk
Other income of 208 Cr represents ~26% of net profit — stripping this out, core operating earnings are less impressive than headline figures suggest
red_flags: Reported D/E of 0.28 masks total debt of 4,606 Cr (likely includes lease liabilities) — true leverage is significantly higher
Finance costs growing at 27.9% CAGR — faster than revenue growth of 13.2% — will compress margins if not managed carefully
Free cash flow has been negative in 4 of last 6 years; the business is consuming capital faster than it generates it
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Aegis Logistics is the type of asset-heavy infrastructure business I generally understand and respect — terminal networks handling hazardous chemicals and LPG are essential services with high switching costs and regulatory protection. The 22.6% net profit CAGR over nine years is genuinely impressive for a business of this nature, and the OCF has been positive every year for the last five. India's growing LPG consumption and petrochemical logistics demand provide a credible long-term growth story.

However, the financial structure gives me pause. The gap between stated borrowings (2,439 Cr) and total debt (4,606 Cr) in FY25 suggests significant off-balance-sheet or lease obligations that are real economic liabilities. Finance costs of 165 Cr in FY25 growing at 27.9% CAGR will become a meaningful drag. At 32x P/E and 23x EV/EBITDA, the stock is priced reasonably but not cheaply for this level of capital intensity and leverage. I would want to see FCF turn sustainably positive and debt growth moderate before becoming enthusiastic.
